title: Store Sales Down After Chuseok? A 5-Step HQ Diagnosis and Defense
description: Post-Chuseok sales dips mix holiday rebounds with real problems. A 5-step HQ playbook to spot at-risk stores, find causes, and prevent the next decline.
html:
Diagnosing and defending against franchise store sales declines after Chuseok

After the holiday, weekly reports mix recovering stores with stores that have real problems

CORE SUMMARY

✓ A sales dip in the first one to two weeks after Chuseok is common; it is safer to judge using numbers from the third week of October onward, once the holiday effect has faded.

✓ Identify declining stores by comparing them against three baselines: the same period last year, the four-week pre-holiday average, and stores in the same trade area.

✓ Break the cause down by traffic and average ticket, channel, time of day, and menu, then layer in operational signals such as reviews, inspection results, and staffing changes to narrow it down.

✓ Defending against declines requires a system that checks, every week, the operational signals that waver before sales do.

Diagnosing a franchise store sales decline means separating temporary fluctuations from store-specific problems among the stores whose sales have dropped, then narrowing down the cause with data. Right after a holiday like Chuseok (Korea’s fall harvest holiday), when spending patterns swing sharply, nearly every store’s numbers move together, which makes this distinction far more important than usual.

It has been almost two weeks since the Chuseok holiday ended. Open your weekly sales report and you will likely find quite a few stores whose sales fell from the previous week. If you respond to all of them the same way, your supervisors’ calendars fill up fast, and the stores that actually need help get pushed down the list. That is why you first need to separate stores that dipped briefly from the holiday rebound from stores that were already sliding before the holiday, with the decline masked by holiday sales.

This article lays out, in five steps, the order in which headquarters should review stores after Chuseok, and it also covers early-signal management to prevent the next decline. The five steps are: ① judge whether the dip is normal, ② select targets using comparison baselines, ③ break down sales, ④ layer in operational signals, and ⑤ classify stores into tiers. Each step uses the results of the previous one to shrink the list of stores to review, so the more stores a franchisor has, the bigger the payoff.

How do you pick out declining franchise stores after Chuseok?

First determine whether the decline is a holiday rebound or a structural decline, then use three comparison baselines to choose which stores to review. Not every decline happens for the same reason, so you need to classify the type of decline before you can set the order of response.

Step 1. Determine whether the post-Chuseok decline is normal

Post-holiday sales declines fall into two broad types. A holiday rebound decline is a temporary dip that occurs when dining-out and gift spending concentrates during the holiday and consumers cut back afterward. Stores in the same region drop by similar amounts together and usually return to normal levels within two to three weeks. A structural decline is a drop driven by problems within the store itself, regardless of the holiday. Only that store falls noticeably, and looking back, it was often already trending down from early September. Holiday sales simply differed from usual and temporarily hid the trend.

TypeCharacteristicsHow to check
A holiday rebound declineStores in the same region drop by similar amounts and recover within 2–3 weeksCheck whether it moves in the same direction as the regional average
A structural declineOnly that store drops, with a downtrend since before the holidayCheck the trend against early-September sales

The shape of the rebound also varies by trade area. Office districts tend to recover quickly once people return to work, while residential areas may see dining out stay down for a while because of holiday spending fatigue. Stores near tourist spots or highways simply return to normal after a big holiday spike, yet compared week over week, that can look like a steep decline. So before looking at the numbers, it helps to consider what kind of trade area each store is in.

Step 2. Pick out declining stores using three comparison baselines

A single week-over-week figure is not enough. If you use a holiday week as the baseline, almost every store looks as if it fell or rose. Look at the three baselines below together.

1

CRITERIA 01

Vs. the same period last year (matched by weekday)

This baseline filters out seasonal and holiday effects. Because holiday dates shift every year, compare by “weeks after the holiday ended” rather than by calendar date for accuracy. Match weekdays as well, since a period with one extra weekend day has an advantage.

2

CRITERIA 02

Vs. the four-week pre-holiday average

This baseline shows the store’s underlying strength just before the holiday. If current sales have nearly returned to this average, the dip is likely a rebound; if the average itself had already fallen below earlier levels, that signals a problem that began before the holiday.

3

CRITERIA 03

Vs. stores in the same trade area or region

This baseline separates a regional problem from a store-specific one. For example, if all stores in a region fell 10% but one store fell 25%, the 15-point gap is what that store needs to explain on its own.

When building comparison values, follow three rules to keep your judgment steady. First, for periods with a different number of operating days, such as closures or remodeling, convert to daily averages. Second, check that the four-week pre-holiday average does not include the peak pre-holiday rush week. Third, review stores opened within the last three months separately, since their sales are still ramping up and should not be measured by the same yardstick. Following just these three rules eliminates much of the misjudgment caused by the numbers themselves.

Prioritize stores that show a decline on two or more of the three baselines. Stores that fell on only one baseline are most likely showing differences caused by trade area or calendar composition.

Layering the three baselines reveals stores hidden by the holiday effect

In what order do you narrow down the causes of a franchise store’s sales decline?

Split sales into customer traffic and average ticket first, then break them down by channel, time of day, and menu, and layer in operational signals beyond sales to narrow down the cause. Since sales equal traffic multiplied by average ticket, which of the two fell determines a completely different direction for your investigation.

Step 3. Break down sales to narrow the cause

Breakdown orderIf you see thisSuspect first
① Traffic / average ticketTraffic downTrade area changes, new competitors, service or quality issues
① Traffic / average ticketAverage ticket downFewer combo and add-on sales, excessive discounting
② Channel (dine-in, delivery, takeout)Only delivery downDelivery app ranking, reviews, delivery times
③ Time of dayOnly weekday lunch downNearby office-worker demand, lunch table turnover
④ MenuOnly signature items downCooking quality, sellouts, recipe compliance

Breaking it down this way turns the vague statement “sales fell” into a specific problem such as “weekday lunch delivery traffic fell.” The more specific the problem, the more specific the response. Conversely, if the decline does not narrow to any one branch and is spread evenly across all channels and times, it is time to suspect a bigger cause, such as a change in the entire trade area or a problem with the store’s image.

When breaking down by channel, don’t treat delivery sales as one lump; split them again into order count and value per order. If order count fell, the problem is likely visibility and reviews; if value per order fell, suspect pricing policies such as minimum order amounts or coupons first. For time of day, separate lunch from dinner and weekdays from weekends to see “which customers dropped off.”

Step 4. Layer in operational signals beyond sales

Sales figures show outcomes, not causes. Causes usually leave traces in store operating records first, so overlay the four items below with the point at which sales turned down.

  • Reviews: Check whether negative reviews increased around the holiday and whether the same complaints, like “smaller portions” or “arrived late,” keep recurring. The content of complaints tells you more than the rating.
  • Inspection results: Check whether any items dropped in recent QSCV (Quality, Service, Cleanliness, Value) inspections and whether flagged issues remain unresolved.
  • Staffing: Check whether experienced staff quit, part-time rosters changed over the holiday, or the store owner is spending more time away from the store.
  • Changes outside the store: Also review notes in supervisor visit records, such as nearby construction, a competing brand opening, or changes in parking.

The real-world challenge: data is scattered across different places

Sales often sit in the POS, reviews on delivery apps and map platforms, and inspection results in supervisors’ individual files or messenger photos. Piecing together one store’s situation can take half a day, and with dozens of stores it is hard to even attempt.

As a result, many franchisors end up judging by sales figures alone and, unable to find the cause, settle for “let’s just run a promotion.” If you can see sales and operating records by store in one place, this process gets much shorter, because the point when sales turned down, when negative reviews rose, and when inspection scores fell all line up at a glance.

Overlaying when sales turned down with when operational signals appeared reveals the cause

How do you separate stores that need different responses despite the same decline?

Looking at how many baselines show a decline alongside whether operational signals are present, two stores that fell by the same amount on paper can lead to completely different conclusions. Sorting those conclusions into three tiers, Watch, Caution, and Intervene, sets the order of supervisor visits.

The same 18% decline, two different conclusions

To illustrate, let’s imagine two stores in the same region. The figures below are examples for explanation only.

Check itemStore A (office district)Store B (residential area)
Vs. previous week-18%-18%
Vs. the four-week pre-holiday average-3%-15%
Vs. regional averageSimilar10 pts lower
Operational signalsNothing unusualKitchen staff replaced in mid-September; more “taste has changed” reviews
AssessmentHoliday rebound, WatchStructural decline, Intervene

Looking only at week-over-week numbers, you would have sent supervisors to both stores with the same priority. But Store A has nearly regained its pre-holiday strength and is moving in line with the region. Store B, on the other hand, was already declining before the holiday, and the timing coincides with the kitchen staff change and the rise in taste-related reviews.

POINT 01

The same 18% decline calls for a different remedy when the cause differs

Store B’s problem is cooking quality, not the holiday, so the response should be recipe retraining, not a promotion. You can only see this difference by looking at comparison baselines and operational signals together.

Step 5. Separate stores to intervene in from stores to watch

You can’t send supervisors to every store, so the goal of this step is to set priorities. The criteria below are examples; adjust them to your brand’s normal range of sales fluctuation.

TierExample criteriaResponse
WatchDecline on only 1 baselineRecheck on the same baselines in 2 weeks
CautionDecline on 2+ baselines, no operational signalsPhone check-in with the store owner to understand the situation
InterveneDecline on 2+ baselines + review, inspection, or staffing signalsSupervisor visit and a 4-week improvement plan

When visiting an Intervene-tier store, it is important to bring the numbers you confirmed in the earlier steps. Ask “Why are sales so bad lately?” and the store owner will likely blame the economy or the weather. But say “Weekday lunch delivery orders are down from before the holiday, and over the same period, reviews mentioning smaller portions have increased,” and the conversation moves straight to solutions. Numbers are an effective tool for getting headquarters and store owners to look at the same thing.

Rather than setting tier criteria once and leaving them, keep calibrating them. At first, too many stores may land in the Caution tier, or almost none. If Caution-tier stores make up a large share of the total, the criteria are too loose; if the Intervene tier stays empty, you may be missing operational signals. Decide first how many visits one supervisor can handle, then tune the criteria so that the Intervene tier fits within that capacity, and you will have a system that is actually used in the field.

Once you have an improvement plan, measure again four weeks later against the same three baselines. Checking improvement on the same baselines lets you build a record of which responses worked for the next quarter.

Once stores are tiered, the order of supervisor visits falls into place naturally

What should you watch to prevent franchise store sales declines in advance?

The key to defending against sales declines is checking, every week, the operational signals that waver before sales do. Sales are an outcome that shows up after problems pile up, so if you start looking for causes only after sales turn down, you have already lost several weeks. In the earlier example, Store B’s reviews worsened first in mid-September when the kitchen staff changed, and sales fell after that.

Early signals of a franchise store sales decline are operational changes that appear before sales drop. Signals worth checking regularly at headquarters include the following.

Early signalWhy it appears firstCheck frequency
Rising share of negative reviews, repeated complaintsCustomers speak up in reviews before they stop coming backWeekly
Accumulating unresolved QSCV inspection itemsQuality and hygiene issues gradually erode repeat visitsRight after inspection
Key staff departures, more owner absencesWhere cooking quality and service start to slipAs needed
Longer prep and delivery timesDirectly affects delivery app visibility and reorder ratesWeekly

Building a defense system takes three steps. First, record the signals above for every store each week using the same criteria. Next, move stores with two or more overlapping signals up to the “Caution” tier and start talking with the store owner before sales fall. Finally, once a month, look back at whether the stores that actually declined had already been flagged as Caution, and refine the criteria. The more you repeat this check, the better your alert criteria will fit your brand.

It is also important to assign an owner to each signal. Reviews go to marketing, inspection results to supervisors, and staffing changes to the assigned supervisor’s notes from store owner meetings; when ownership of each record is clear, weekly checks don’t fizzle out. If you also designate someone to consolidate the results into a single weekly list, you spend less meeting time debating where the numbers came from.

How can you reduce the work of collecting early signals every week?

The practical difficulty is that gathering these signals by hand for every store is not easy. When inspection records, sales, and store information are scattered, it is hard to stick to the check schedule, and you end up looking only after sales have already fallen. That is why more franchisors are adopting operations systems that bring HQ work together in one place.

In its operations management area, it records and tracks QSCV inspections of franchise stores and manages POS sales aggregation and store information on HQ’s terms. When inspection results are tracked by store instead of sitting in documents, and sales and store information are organized on the same basis, checking the early signals above every week becomes much easier. A screen showing sales and operational signals by store together (example screen: FDAM)

October sales review: what to do and when?

TimingTo-do
Week 2, OctClassify stores by trade area; calculate the 4-week pre-holiday average
Week 3, OctSelect declining stores using the three baselines; break down sales
Week 4, OctCheck operational signals, assign tiers, visit Intervene-tier stores
Week 3, NovRemeasure Intervene-tier stores; final check before the year-end peak

Following this schedule lets you confirm improvement results at problem stores before the year-end peak season begins. Once peak season starts, sales rise across the board, making it easy for problem stores to hide behind the numbers again. October is close to your last chance to pick out the problems.

Frequently asked questions

Q. By what percentage must a store’s sales fall before headquarters intervenes?

There is no fixed threshold that fits every brand. It is more accurate to look at whether the drop is significantly larger than the brand’s average fluctuation, how many of the three baselines show a decline, and whether operational signals appear at the same time.

Q. When do sales usually recover after Chuseok?

If it is a holiday rebound decline, sales usually return to pre-holiday levels within two to three weeks. If sales are still below the four-week pre-holiday average three weeks after the holiday ends, it is worth suspecting a structural decline.

Q. If only delivery sales fell, what should you check first?

Look first at delivery app ranking, recent reviews, and changes in prep and delivery times. If dine-in sales are fine, the problem is more likely in the delivery channel than in store quality.

Q. What should headquarters do every week to defend against store sales declines?

Record four early signals for each store, namely the share of negative reviews, unresolved inspection items, key staffing changes, and delivery times, and start conversations with stores showing two or more overlapping signals before sales fall. Once a month, review whether the stores that actually declined were caught in advance, and refine the criteria.

Most franchise store sales declines after Chuseok are passing phenomena. But mixed in are stores with real problems, and these will hide behind the numbers again during the year-end peak. When the third week of October’s numbers come in, run through the five steps outlined here, and keep the signals you find as weekly check items to prevent the next decline.
